solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Limp I had after cold gets into back muscle

indicators.note: after places the contracted I had at the end, behind the rest
gets into says the cold letter goes inside the reversed muscle
back tells us to read the muscle word from end to start

parts.note: the calf is the muscle at the back of the lower leg
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
I had contracts to I'd, giving these letters

explanation.surface: Someone with a floppy, weakened back muscle after catching a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the muscle to give FLAC, and 'gets into' slips the cold letter inside it; 'after' puts the contraction at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something flaccid hangs loose and lacks firmness, just as a limp thing does.

clue.text: Unable to move foot, when entering

indicators.note: entering says the word for when goes into the abbreviation for foot

parts.note: FT is the usual abbreviation for foot, the unit of length
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: A foot stuck fast just as it is being put in somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuck fast means firmly fixed, unable to shift, as in a ship held fast on rocks.

clue.text: A trick shot on area of snooker table gets built up

parts.note: a massé is a trick shot in billiards or snooker, played with a steeply raised cue to swerve the ball
the D is the semicircular area marked at the baulk end of a snooker table

explanation.surface: A snooker player builds up a break with a flashy shot from the baulk area.
explanation.walkthrough: On a snooker table the D is the half-circle from which a player restarts after potting the white.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to amass is to accumulate or pile up, so amassed means accumulated.

clue.text: Complaint: it's endlessly chilly and frosty

indicators.note: endlessly says each of the two describing words loses its final letter

parts.note: chilly means cold
frosty means icy

explanation.surface: Someone grumbling that the weather is never-ending cold and frosty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' governs both words: COLD loses D and ICY loses Y, leaving COL + IC.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint here is an ailment; colic is severe abdominal pain, a classic infant illness.

clue.text: What may suffer from mangled feet and badly gored leg?

definitions.text: What may suffer from mangled feet

indicators.note: badly signals that the words gored leg are to be rearranged into a damaged order

explanation.surface: An injured person whose feet are mangled and whose leg has been gored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feet' are metrical feet: poor verse is often clumsy in rhythm. The surface sends the reader to a bullfight.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggerel is badly written comic verse, whose metre is often lame and irregular.

clue.text: Composer available from PC World?

parts.note: PC stands for police constable, a cop
a world, as in 'a land of dreams', can be a land

explanation.surface: A shopper asking whether something can be bought at the computer retailer PC World.
explanation.walkthrough: PC World is a British computer and electronics chain; here PC is a police constable.
explanation.definitionFit: Aaron Copland was an American composer, known for Appalachian Spring and Fanfare for the Common Man.

clue.text: Vessel with zigzagging course almost capsized rest

indicators.note: capsized, in a down clue, says the whole assembly is turned upside down

parts.note: a pan is a cooking vessel

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the sailing course is dropped

parts.note: a tack is a sailing course across the wind, and tacking makes a zigzag

explanation.surface: A boat zigzagging into the wind nearly turned over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts TACK to TAC; 'capsized' turns PAN + TAC over to read CAT NAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A catnap is a short sleep, a brief rest.

clue.text: Might it save one's bacon?

parts.note: to save one's bacon is to rescue oneself from trouble; read literally, a pig-shaped money box saves, and pigs give bacon

explanation.definitionFit: A pig-shaped money box is where a child saves coins, and pigs are the source of bacon.

clue.text: Elite RA works here?

indicators.note: works, as in the clay worked into shape, signals that Elite RA is rearranged

explanation.surface: Suggesting where a top Royal Academician might do their painting.
explanation.walkthrough: RA is a Royal Academician, a member of Britain's Royal Academy of Arts. 'works' is the anagram signal and also the verb of the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An atelier is an artist's studio or workshop, just where an eminent painter would work.

clue.text: Wants statistics about European team second in group

indicators.note: about says the statistics word goes around the other pieces

parts.note: statistics are data
a side is a team, as in football

indicators.note: second in means take the second letter of the word group

explanation.surface: A manager wanting figures on a European team placed second in its group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' has the statistics word wrap the rest, which goes in after its first letter. 'second in group' is a letter, not a league placing.
explanation.definitionFit: Desiderata are things wanted or needed, from Latin for 'things desired'.

clue.text: Sailor surrounded by minor celestial illumination

indicators.note: surrounded by says the sailor word sits inside the word for minor

parts.note: minor means slight, small
a tar is a sailor, as in Jack Tar

explanation.surface: A sailor at night lit only faintly by the heavens.
explanation.definitionFit: Light shining from stars is a form of illumination coming from the heavens.

clue.text: Party-goer's setting aside time to have a shot

indicators.note: setting aside says the time letter is removed

parts.note: a party-goer is a guest; with the apostrophe s it gives the letters of guests

explanation.surface: A party guest putting time aside to take a drink or have a go at something.
explanation.walkthrough: GUEST'S loses its T, the one in the middle, giving GUESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to have a shot at something is to attempt it, as when you guess an answer.

clue.text: What might ornithologist see in Africa? "Redbreast", I cry incorrectly

definitions.text: What might ornithologist see in Africa?

indicators.note: incorrectly says the letters of Redbreast and I cry are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher in Africa misidentifying a bird, crying 'robin redbreast!' by mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: The secretary bird is a long-legged African bird of prey, so a birder there might spot one.

clue.text: Welcome record of voyage perhaps in authentic tourist's memoir

indicators.note: in says the welcome and record words go inside the word for authentic

parts.note: authentic means true
ave is a Latin greeting, hail or welcome
a log is a ship's record of a voyage

explanation.surface: A traveller's welcome record of a sea voyage in a genuine memoir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welcome' reads as an adjective praising the record, but it is the Latin greeting ave.
explanation.definitionFit: A travelogue is a film, talk or account of someone's travels, a tourist's narrative.

clue.text: Flushed wine and coffee in opposite directions

parts.note: red is a type of wine

indicators.note: in opposite directions says the second word runs the other way from the first

parts.note: decaf is decaffeinated coffee

explanation.surface: Someone flushed after drinking wine and coffee mixed together.
explanation.walkthrough: RED reads forwards; DECAF reads the opposite way, giving FACED.
explanation.definitionFit: Flushed and red-faced both describe a face reddened with blood, from embarrassment or heat.

clue.text: Commercial exploitation's closing gold mining resource with wearying regularity

parts.note: a commercial is an advertisement, an ad
the closing letter of the word exploitation
AU is the chemical symbol for gold
a seam is a layer of coal or ore that is mined

explanation.surface: An advert about ending exploitation of a gold mine, repeated tiresomely.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means 'to the point of nausea', so something done until it becomes tiresome.

clue.text: More light from flames either side of a river

indicators.note: either side of says the flames word is split to sit on both sides of the letter a

parts.note: flames make up a fire

explanation.surface: Flames on both banks of a river making it brighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'either side of' splits FIRE around A to make FAIRE, then R follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair can mean pale or light in colouring, so the comparative means lighter.

clue.text: Reduced watts before reversing current in transformer

parts.note: W, the abbreviated form of watts
ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: reversing says the current word is read backwards

parts.note: a current is a flow

explanation.surface: Electrical talk about watts and current reversing in a transformer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about electrics, but 'transformer' is a shape-shifter.
explanation.definitionFit: A werewolf is a human who changes shape into a wolf, so it transforms.

clue.text: One's fleeced by grasping copper, the head of narcotics

indicators.note: grasping says the word for by holds the copper and the narcotics letter

parts.note: via means by way of
CU is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: head of says take the first letter of the word narcotics

explanation.surface: Someone cheated out of money by a policeman who is also a drug boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman, but it is the metal. 'One's fleeced' means one is shorn, not swindled.
explanation.definitionFit: The vicuña is a South American relative of the llama, prized and shorn for its fine wool.

clue.text: Note major road turning between church and a castle in Spain

indicators.note: between says the reversed letters sit between the church and the a
turning says the note and the road are read backwards

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
the M1 is Britain's main motorway, with the 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Directions: a note, a main road turning between a church and a Spanish castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'castle in Spain' looks like a place, but it is an idiom for an impossible dream.
explanation.definitionFit: A castle in Spain is a daydream or fanciful scheme; a chimera is likewise an illusion.

clue.text: Moulded askew, container displays flaw

indicators.note: moulded means reshaped, so the letters of askew are formed anew

parts.note: a pot is a container

explanation.surface: A misshapen pot whose moulding went askew shows a defect.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a weak spot is a point of vulnerability, a flaw in something otherwise sound.

clue.text: City, supremely faultless, knocking out United — no upset

indicators.note: knocking out says the United letter is removed

parts.note: purest means most faultless, the superlative of pure
U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names

indicators.note: upset, in a down clue, means turned upside down, reading the word no backwards

explanation.surface: A football report: a perfect city side beat United with no upset.
explanation.walkthrough: Preston North End beating Manchester United is the surface; Preston is a city in Lancashire, northwest England.
explanation.definitionFit: Preston is a city in Lancashire in north-west England.

clue.text: Civil engineer in Slough's making barriers

indicators.note: in says the engineer letters are placed inside the marsh word

parts.note: a slough is a swamp, so sloughs are fens

explanation.surface: A civil engineer at work in Slough putting up barriers.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is an English town west of London, but here it is a bog, so 'Slough's' reads as plural sloughs.
explanation.definitionFit: Fences are barriers that enclose or keep things out.

clue.text: Bloomers to be worn for certain around new sports facility

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers (bloomers) worn round the neck

indicators.note: around says the word for certain is split to go round the word for new

parts.note: certain means sure
recent means new

explanation.surface: Bloomers, the baggy undergarments, that must be worn at a new sports centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' are flowers, not knickers. 'around' splits the word for certain after its second letter to hold the word for new.
explanation.definitionFit: A leisure centre is a public building with a pool, gym and courts for sport and recreation.

clue.text: Sound of fierce creature in northern habitat

indicators.note: sound of says the answer is pronounced like the word for the fierce creature

parts.note: a tiger is a fierce animal

explanation.surface: Hearing the call of a fierce beast in a northern wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: This works in a British, non-rhotic accent, where the two words sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The taiga is the vast swampy coniferous forest belt of subarctic Russia and Canada.

clue.text: Address covering a river of Eurasia

indicators.note: covering says the address letters go round the a

parts.note: a URL is a web address

explanation.surface: A speech covering a river that crosses Europe and Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ural river flows from the Ural Mountains through Russia and Kazakhstan to the Caspian, on the Europe-Asia boundary.

clue.text: On reflection, some of these Egyptian birds from Canada?

indicators.note: On reflection says the hidden letters are read backwards
some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Thinking it over, perhaps some of these birds are Egyptian rather than Canadian.
explanation.walkthrough: The Egyptian goose is a real bird, which helps the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Canada geese are the familiar large waterfowl native to North America, so they are birds from Canada.

clue.text: Cutting 500 smash hit records for singer

indicators.note: smash says the letters of hit records are broken up and rearranged
cutting says the Roman five hundred is taken out of the pool of letters

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: A band cutting 500 copies of a smash hit record for its singer.
explanation.walkthrough: HIT RECORDS minus D leaves HITRECORS, rearranged by 'smash'. 'Cutting' and 'records' pose as recording-studio talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A chorister is a member of a choir, a singer.

clue.text: Scholar's problems are returning

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the definition is just the scholar

indicators.note: returning says the words for problems and are are read backwards together

parts.note: sums are arithmetic problems

explanation.surface: An academic's problems keep coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: SUMS ARE read backwards gives ERA SMUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Desiderius Erasmus was the Dutch Renaissance humanist scholar.

clue.text: Flatter woman in fine lines

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils

indicators.note: in says the woman's name sits inside the fine and lines letters

parts.note: Anne is a woman's name

explanation.surface: Praising a woman dressed in fine-striped clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flatter' looks like 'more flat', but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Flannel as a verb is British slang for flattering or sweet-talking someone with insincere words.
